title: Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt
summary: How Wangari Maathai of Kenya started the Green Belt Movement, which trained women to plant tens of millions of trees, and became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
poll: One person can make a big difference for the environment.

versions.title: Wangari and the Trees
versions.text:
Wangari Maathai was born in Kenya in 1940. As a girl, she lived on a farm. She drank from a clear stream. Big trees grew all round.

She loved to learn. She went to school in the USA. Then she came home. She got the top degree a school gives. She was the first woman in her part of the world to do so.

But the land had changed. Lots of trees were cut down. Streams dried up. Rain took the soil. Moms had to walk far for wood.

She had a plan. Plant trees! In 1977, she began a group. It was the Green Belt Movement. Moms grew small trees from seeds. These are seedlings. They got paid for each tree that lived.

The trees did lots of good. Their roots held the soil. They gave shade, wood, and fruit. The group planted lots of trees.

In 2004, she won a big prize. It was the Nobel Peace Prize. She was the first African woman to win it.

She told of a fire in the woods. A small bird brings drops to it. It says, "I do the best I can." We can be like that bird.

Wangari Maathai was born in 1940 in Kenya, a country in East Africa. She grew up on a farm in the green hills, where she drank clean water from a nearby stream. Tall trees and thick plants grew all around her family's home.

Wangari was an excellent student. She won a scholarship to study biology at a college in the United States. Later, she returned to Kenya and continued her studies. In 1971, she became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, the highest university degree.

When she visited the countryside, she saw that her land had changed. Many forests had been cleared to make room for farms. Streams were drying up. Without tree roots to hold it, the soil washed away in the rain. This loss of soil is called erosion. Women told her they had to walk for hours to collect firewood.

Wangari had a simple solution: plant trees. In 1977, she started the Green Belt Movement. The movement taught women to grow seedlings, which are young trees grown from seeds. The women planted the seedlings and were paid a small amount for each tree that survived.

The trees improved the environment in many ways. Their roots held the soil in place and helped rain soak into the ground. They also provided shade, firewood, and fruit. Over the years, the movement planted tens of millions of trees across Kenya.

In 2004, Wangari won the Nobel Peace Prize. She was the first African woman to receive it. She died in 2011, but the movement continues her work.

Wangari often told a story about a forest fire. All the animals run away, except a tiny hummingbird. It carries drops of water to the fire, one by one. "I am doing the best I can," the bird says. Today, many countries, including Saudi Arabia, have plans to plant billions of trees.

versions.title: Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt
versions.text:
Wangari Maathai was born in 1940 within Kenya, a nation situated in East Africa, and she grew up on a farm nestled within the fertile highlands, where she drank clean, unpolluted water from a nearby stream and where towering trees and dense vegetation surrounded her family's modest home throughout her childhood.

Wangari proved a very gifted student, ultimately earning a scholarship to study biology at a college located within the United States. Later, she returned to Kenya to continue her advanced education, and in 1971 she became the very first woman throughout East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, the highest academic degree conferred by any university.

Traveling extensively through the surrounding countryside, she observed with growing alarm that the landscape had been greatly and irreversibly transformed. Extensive forests had been cleared to create additional agricultural land, and once-steady streams were gradually disappearing entirely; lacking tree roots to anchor it firmly in place, the exposed soil washed away rapidly during heavy rainfall, a destructive geological process officially known as erosion. Rural women explained, with evident frustration, that they were now compelled to walk for many hours simply to collect firewood, and that their families consequently faced increasingly limited access to nutritious, steady food sources.

Wangari proposed a straightforward yet profoundly effective solution: plant trees. In 1977, she officially founded the Green Belt Movement, an organization specifically designed to train women to cultivate seedlings and later plant them throughout their own local communities. Each participating woman received a modest financial payment for every tree that survived, so the initiative also restored badly damaged land while also providing a valuable, independent source of personal income.

The newly planted trees improved the surrounding environment in many interconnected ways. Their extensive root systems stabilized the soil and permitted rainwater to penetrate deeply into the ground. Meanwhile, their spreading branches provided welcome shade, essential firewood, and nutritious fruit. Across subsequent decades, the movement collectively planted tens of millions of trees throughout Kenya, demonstrating that sustainable environmental transformation can originate organically with ordinary individuals rather than only with powerful governmental institutions.

In 2004, Wangari was officially awarded the prestigious Nobel Peace Prize, becoming the very first African woman to receive this distinguished international honor, which explicitly recognized that responsible, careful management of natural resources can contribute to building peaceful societies. Two years later, her inspiring example motivated a bold international campaign to plant a full billion trees worldwide. This famous environmentalist died in 2011. Yet the Green Belt Movement continues faithfully carrying forward her great, lasting work.

Wangari frequently recounted an instructive parable concerning a devastating forest fire. While every other frightened animal flees the advancing flames, a diminutive hummingbird carries individual drops of water toward the fire, one by one, explaining simply, "I am doing the best I can." Today, many countries across the globe, including Saudi Arabia, have announced bold plans to plant billions of additional trees, thereby continuing within their own communities the environmental vision she so passionately championed throughout her remarkable life.

versions.title: Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt
versions.text:
Wangari Maathai was born in 1940 within Kenya, a nation situated in East Africa, and she grew up on a modest farm nestled within the fertile highlands, where she drank clean, entirely unpolluted water from a nearby stream and where towering trees and dense, abundant vegetation surrounded her family's humble home throughout her entire formative childhood.

Wangari proved an exceptionally gifted and academically distinguished student, ultimately earning a competitive scholarship to study biology at a college located within the United States. Subsequently, she returned to Kenya to continue her advanced graduate education, and in 1971 she became the very first woman throughout the entirety of East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, the highest academic degree conferred by any university anywhere.

Traveling extensively through the surrounding Kenyan countryside, she observed with mounting alarm that the once-familiar landscape had been dramatically and seemingly irreversibly transformed. Extensive native forests had been systematically cleared to create additional agricultural farmland, and once-reliable streams were gradually disappearing entirely from the landscape; lacking tree roots to anchor it securely in place, the newly exposed soil washed away rapidly during periods of heavy rainfall, a destructive geological process formally termed erosion. Rural women explained to her, with evident and understandable frustration, that they were now compelled to walk for many exhausting hours simply to collect basic firewood, and that their families consequently faced increasingly limited access to nutritious, dependable food sources.

Wangari proposed a deceptively straightforward yet ultimately profoundly transformative solution: systematically plant trees throughout the affected regions. In 1977, she formally founded the Green Belt Movement, a grassroots organization specifically designed to train local women to cultivate tree seedlings and subsequently plant them throughout their own immediate communities. Each participating woman received a modest financial payment for every tree that successfully survived to maturity, so the initiative simultaneously restored severely degraded land while also providing a genuinely valuable, independent source of personal income for participants.

The newly planted trees improved the surrounding natural environment in numerous interconnected and mutually reinforcing ways. Their extensive, deep root systems effectively stabilized the loosened soil and permitted rainwater to penetrate deeply into the ground rather than simply washing away, while their spreading branches provided welcome shade, essential firewood, and nutritious fruit for local families. Across subsequent decades, the movement collectively planted tens of millions of individual trees throughout Kenya, conclusively demonstrating that genuinely sustainable environmental transformation can originate organically with ordinary individuals and local communities rather than exclusively with powerful, distant governmental institutions.

In 2004, Wangari was formally awarded the prestigious Nobel Peace Prize, thereby becoming the very first African woman in history to receive this distinguished international honor, which explicitly and deliberately recognized that responsible, careful stewardship of natural resources can meaningfully contribute to building genuinely peaceful, stable societies. Two years thereafter, her inspiring personal example motivated an ambitious international campaign to plant a full billion trees worldwide, extending her vision far beyond Kenya's borders. This celebrated environmentalist died in 2011, yet the Green Belt Movement she founded continues faithfully carrying forward her extraordinary, lasting legacy of work.

Wangari frequently recounted an instructive parable concerning a devastating forest fire that she found personally meaningful. While every other frightened forest animal flees desperately from the advancing flames, a diminutive hummingbird persistently and tirelessly carries individual drops of water toward the fire, one by one, explaining simply and without pretense, "I am doing the best I can." Today, numerous countries across the entire globe, including Saudi Arabia, have announced genuinely ambitious national plans to plant billions of additional trees, thereby continuing within their own communities the environmental vision she so passionately championed throughout her remarkable, consequential life.

wrong.C: 2004 is when she won the Nobel Peace Prize.

questions.stem: What was Wangari the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn?
options: A doctorate
A gold medal in sports
A scholarship
A large farm
questions.why: The article says she was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate.

wrong.C: She won a scholarship, but the article does not say she was the first.
wrong.D: She grew up on a farm; she did not earn one.

questions.stem: What does erosion mean in the article?
options: Planting trees in rows
A kind of firewood
The washing away of soil
A long walk to a stream
questions.why: The article says that when soil washed away in the rain, this loss of soil was called erosion.

wrong.A: Planting trees was the solution to erosion.
wrong.D: The long walks were for firewood, and they are not erosion.

questions.stem: Why were streams drying up and soil washing away?
options: Too many trees had been planted.
Women collected too much water.
Hummingbirds drank from the streams.
Forests had been cleared for farmland.
questions.why: The article says forests had been cleared for farms, and without roots the soil washed away.

wrong.A: Planting trees helped; it did not cause the problem.
wrong.B: The article does not blame women for the problem.
wrong.C: Hummingbirds appear only in a story about a fire.

questions.stem: Why was paying women for each surviving tree a smart idea?
options: It gave them a reason to care for the trees.
It made the trees grow much faster.
It meant they did not need firewood.
It helped them win the Nobel Prize.
questions.why: The women were paid only when a tree survived, so they had a reason to look after it, and they also earned money.

wrong.B: Money does not make trees grow faster.
wrong.C: The trees later provided firewood; payment did not remove the need for it.
wrong.D: Wangari, not each woman, won the prize.

questions.stem: What does the hummingbird story suggest about Wangari's beliefs?
options: She thought only leaders could solve problems.
She believed fires were good for forests.
She believed every person's effort matters.
She thought birds should put out fires.
questions.why: The tiny bird does the best it can, which matches Wangari's belief that each person can help.

wrong.A: Her movement relied on ordinary women, not only leaders.
wrong.B: The bird tries to stop the fire, so fire is the problem.
wrong.D: The story is a lesson about people, not a plan for birds.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly organized?
options: As a list of different types of trees
In time order, following Wangari's life and work
As a comparison of Kenya and the United States
As a set of steps for planting a tree
questions.why: The article moves from her birth in 1940 to her studies, the movement in 1977, the prize in 2004, and her death in 2011.

wrong.A: The article does not list types of trees.
wrong.C: The United States is mentioned only as where she studied.
wrong.D: The article does not give planting steps.

MID.prompt: Explain how planting trees helped both the land and the women of Kenya. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained how the trees helped the land.
I explained how the movement helped the women.
I supported my ideas with details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Planting trees helped the land because tree roots hold the soil in place and help rainwater soak into the ground, which stopped the erosion that was washing away the soil when forests were cleared. Planting trees also helped the women of Kenya, because the Green Belt Movement taught them to grow seedlings and paid them a small amount for each tree that survived, giving them income while also saving them from walking for hours to collect firewood. In both ways, the movement improved the environment and the lives of the women who built it.

keyWords.definition: the gradual removal of soil or rock by water, wind, or ice
keyWords.example: Coastal erosion slowly moved the shoreline closer to the road.

keyWords.definition: a person who works to protect the natural world
keyWords.example: The environmentalist spoke to students about saving the mangroves.

keyWords.definition: the highest degree a university gives, earned after years of advanced study and research
keyWords.example: My aunt earned her doctorate in chemistry after six years of research.

keyWords.definition: able to continue for a long time without using up or harming natural resources
keyWords.example: Drip irrigation is a sustainable way to grow crops in dry regions.

keyWords.definition: a group of people who live in the same area or share common interests
keyWords.example: The whole community helped rebuild the market after the storm.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Ordinary people planting trees can restore land and improve lives.
Wangari Maathai is remembered mainly for her studies in the United States.
The Nobel Peace Prize is usually given to scientists who study biology.
Saudi Arabia started the world's first large tree-planting program.
questions.why: The article shows how the Green Belt Movement's tree planting fought erosion and supported women, earning worldwide recognition.

wrong.B: Her studies are background; her movement is the focus.
wrong.C: The article makes no claim about who usually wins the prize.
wrong.D: Saudi Arabia's plans are mentioned as a modern example, not as the first.

questions.stem: Besides the long walks for firewood, what problem did rural women describe?

Forests growing too close to homes
Less nutritious food for their families
Schools that were too crowded

wrong.B: Forests had been cleared, not grown closer.

questions.stem: According to the article, what did the Nobel Peace Prize recognize?
options: That trees grow best in highlands
That protecting nature can support peace
That Kenya has Africa's largest forests
That every woman should study biology
questions.why: The article says the prize recognized that caring for the environment and natural resources can support peaceful societies.

wrong.A: The highlands are where she grew up, not the reason for the prize.
wrong.C: The article makes no claim about forest size.
wrong.D: Her biology studies are not the reason given for the prize.

questions.stem: "Their roots stabilized the soil." What does stabilized mean?
options: Softened
Heated
Removed
Anchored
questions.why: Roots stopped the soil from washing away, so stabilized means held firmly, or anchored, in place.

wrong.A: Softening soil would make erosion worse.
wrong.C: Removing soil is erosion, the opposite of what roots do.

questions.stem: What happened because forests were cleared for farmland?
options: Streams grew larger and deeper.
Women had more firewood.
Soil washed away in heavy rain.
More rain began to fall each year.
questions.why: Without tree roots to anchor it, the soil washed away during heavy rain, a process called erosion.

wrong.B: Women had to walk for hours to find firewood.
wrong.D: The article does not say rainfall increased.

questions.stem: The article says sustainable change can begin with ordinary people. Which detail best supports this idea?
options: Wangari studied biology in the United States.
Rural women planted tens of millions of trees.
Wangari died in the year 2011.
Saudi Arabia has a plan to plant trees.
questions.why: The trees were planted by ordinary women in their communities, which shows change growing from everyday people.

wrong.A: Her education is not an example of ordinary people creating change.
wrong.C: The date of her death does not support this idea.
wrong.D: A national plan comes from a government, not ordinary individuals.

questions.stem: Why might Wangari have told the hummingbird story so often?
options: To warn people about birds that are dangerous
To explain how forest fires start
To show that animals are smarter than people are
To encourage people to act even against huge problems
questions.why: The hummingbird keeps helping against a huge fire, just as Wangari asked people to keep planting trees despite huge problems.

wrong.A: The hummingbird is a hero, not a danger.
wrong.B: The story does not explain how fires start.
wrong.C: The story compares effort, not intelligence.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention Saudi Arabia's tree-planting plans at the end?
options: To show that Wangari's idea still matters today
To compare the weather of Kenya and Saudi Arabia
To argue that every country should copy Kenya
To explain how hummingbirds survive in deserts
questions.why: Mentioning current tree-planting plans connects Wangari's vision to the present day and to readers in Saudi Arabia.

wrong.C: The author does not argue that countries must copy Kenya.
wrong.D: Hummingbirds in deserts are not discussed.

HIGH.prompt: Wangari's hummingbird said, "I am doing the best I can." Is one person's effort enough to solve big environmental problems? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I do not think one person's effort alone is enough to solve big environmental problems, but Wangari Maathai's story shows that one person's effort can start a movement big enough to matter. She founded the Green Belt Movement by teaching women to plant seedlings, and over the years that single idea grew into tens of millions of trees planted across Kenya, showing real change at a huge scale. Still, this result depended on an entire community of women working together for decades, which is really the lesson of the hummingbird story, that each small effort matters most when many people add theirs together.
